rules.title: Defining relative clauses
rules.description:
**The idea** — A defining relative clause tells the listener which person or thing you mean. Without it the noun would be unclear. The clause comes right after the noun and starts with a relative pronoun.

**The form**
- People: `who` or `that`: `the woman who works here`
- Things and animals: `which` or `that`: `the book which I read`
- Possession: `whose` + noun: `the man whose car was stolen`
- Places: `where`; times: `when`; reasons: `why`
- No commas around the clause
- The pronoun replaces the noun, so do not repeat it: no `she`, `it`, `them` after it
- The pronoun can be left out when it is the object: `the book I read`, `the man you met`; never when it is the subject
- The verb agrees with the noun before the pronoun

**When it applies**
- Identifying a noun: signal words `the one who`, `the thing that`, `a person who`
- Definitions: `a mechanic is a person who ...`
- Choosing between similar things

**When it does NOT apply** — If the clause only adds extra information and is set off by commas, use a non-defining clause, where `that` is not possible. Test: if you can delete the clause and the noun is still clear, it is non-defining; if you cannot, it is defining.

**Typical mistakes**
- Repeating the noun with a pronoun (`the car that I bought it`), because the sentence is built like a main clause
- Using `which` for people and `who` for things
- Using `what` as a relative pronoun (`the book what`)
- Adding commas that make the clause non-defining
- Singular verb after a plural antecedent

**Register and usage** — `that` is neutral; `who` and `which` are slightly more formal.

rules.title: The simple passive
rules.description:
**The idea** — In the passive the subject of the sentence is the person or thing that receives the action. English uses it when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, or when you want to begin with the thing affected.

**The form**
- Present passive: `am/is/are` + past participle: `is made`, `are sold`
- Past passive: `was/were` + past participle: `was built`, `were taken`
- Negative: `is not`, `was not` + participle; question: `Is it made ...?`, `where were they taken`
- The doer, if mentioned, comes after `by`: `by the police`
- The participle is the third form of the verb: regular `-ed`, irregular `stolen`, `written`
- `be` agrees with the new subject, not with the doer

**When it applies**
- The doer is unknown or unimportant: signal words `was stolen`, `is made`, `are spoken`
- Processes, facts and news: `is produced in`, `was founded in`
- Formal and written texts, signs, instructions

**When it does NOT apply** — If the doer is the important subject, use the active form; intransitive verbs (`arrive`, `happen`) have no passive. Test: if the sentence needs an object that becomes the subject, the passive is possible; if there is no object, it is not.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the base form or the active form after `be` (`was break`), instead of the participle
- Using the wrong `be` (`letters was sent`) because the doer or the last noun is used for agreement
- Using `did` for a negative passive (`didn't made`)
- Mixing up `by` with other prepositions

**Register and usage** — The passive is common in news, science and formal writing and less so in casual speech.

rules.title: Question tags
rules.description:
**The idea** — A question tag is a short question added to a statement. The speaker uses it to check information or to ask the listener to agree. English builds the tag from the helper verb of the statement, turned around, with the opposite polarity.

**The form**
- Positive statement + negative tag: `are tired`, `aren't you`
- Negative statement + positive tag: `aren't tired`, `are you`
- The tag uses the same auxiliary as the statement: `is`, `has`, `can`, `will`, `would`
- With no auxiliary (present simple), use `do` / `does`; for the past simple use `did`
- The tag has a pronoun subject, never a noun: `it`, `he`, `they`
- Special tags: `I am` → `aren't I`; `let's` → `shall we`; imperatives → `will you` / `won't you`
- Words with a negative meaning (`never`, `hardly`, `nobody`, `nothing`) count as negative: positive tag
- `Everyone`, `nobody`, `someone` take `they`; `nothing`, `something` take `it`

**When it applies**
- Checking facts you are nearly sure of (falling intonation)
- Asking for agreement or confirmation (rising or falling tone)
- Making polite requests and invitations

**When it does NOT apply** — For a real question without an expected answer, use a normal question or a yes/no question. Test: if you expect "yes", use a tag; if you do not know, ask directly.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the same polarity (`are tired, are you`): this only appears in special tones
- Repeating the main verb instead of the auxiliary
- Forgetting `do` / `does` / `did` for the simple tenses
- Using a noun, or the wrong pronoun, in the tag

**Register and usage** — Very common in spoken English, much less in formal writing. Intonation changes the meaning from a real question to a request for agreement.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Let's` takes `shall we`; imperatives take `will you` or `won't you`
- American speakers also use `right?` and `OK?` as tags

rules.title: Reported statements and backshift
rules.description:
**The idea** — When you report what someone said, you tell it from a later point in time. Because of this shift, the verb usually moves one step back into the past, and pronouns and time words change to fit the new speaker.

**The form**
- Reporting verb + (`that`) + clause: `she said that ...`, `he told me that ...`
- `say` has no object; `tell` needs a person: `said`, but `told me`, `told him`
- Backshift: present simple becomes past simple; present continuous becomes past continuous; present perfect and past simple become past perfect
- Modals: `will` becomes `would`, `can` becomes `could`, `may` becomes `might`; `must` often becomes `had to`
- Pronouns follow the new speaker; time words shift: `today` becomes `that day`, `tomorrow` becomes `the next day`, `now` becomes `then`
- Word order stays that of a statement; there are no quotation marks

**When it applies**
- Reporting past speech or thought: signal words `said`, `told`, `explained`, `mentioned`
- News, messages and retelling of conversations

**When it does NOT apply** — If the reporting is in the present (`she says`) or the fact is still true and just said, the tense can stay unchanged. Test: if the reporting verb is past, move the tense back; if it is present, keep it.

**Typical mistakes**
- Keeping the original present tense after `said`, because the fact feels current
- Using `said me` or `told that` without the person; `tell` needs an object and `say` does not
- Forgetting to change pronouns and time words
- Changing the tense only in one verb of a long report

**Register and usage** — In casual speech people often keep the original tense for fresh news; careful writing shifts it.

rules.title: Present tense in future time clauses
rules.description:
**The idea** — When we talk about the future after a time word such as `when` or `as soon as`, English does not repeat `will`. The main clause already says that the action is in the future, so the time clause uses a present form. The same is true for `if`.

**The form**
- main clause: `will` + base verb (or `going to`, or an imperative)
- time clause: conjunction + subject + present simple
- the time clause can come first, with a comma, or second, without one
- present simple has `-s` after he, she, it
- negative time clause: `do not` / `does not` + base verb
- present perfect is possible after `when`, `after`, `until`, `as soon as`: `have` / `has` + past participle
- never `will` or `going to` right after the conjunction

**When it applies**
- Conjunctions of time: `when`, `as soon as`, `before`, `after`, `until`, `while`, `once`, `by the time`
- The condition conjunction `if` and `unless`
- Promises, plans and predictions about the future

**When it does NOT apply** — A question word clause that asks for information keeps `will`, such as `I don't know when she will come`. Test: is the clause a time condition for another action (use the present), or is it the object of a verb like know or ask (the future form stays)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `will` in the time clause: the learner copies the main clause form
- Using `going to` after the conjunction
- Dropping the third person `-s`
- Using `will` with `if` as well
- Choosing the present perfect when two actions happen at the same time

**Register and usage** — Neutral in all registers. In writing, the present perfect after `once` and `after` shows that the first action is finished.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `when` as a question word keeps `will`
- `if` meaning `whether` keeps `will` too

rules.title: Mustn't or don't have to
rules.description:
**The idea** — In the positive, `must` and `have to` are close. In the negative they split completely. `mustn't` says that something is forbidden; `don't have to` says that something is not necessary but still allowed. Mixing them reverses the meaning.

**The form**
- `mustn't` (or `must not`) + base verb: prohibition
- `don't have to` / `doesn't have to` + base verb: no obligation
- `must` has one form for every person; it has no `-s`, no past form of its own
- `have to` is an ordinary verb: `has to` after he, she, it
- question with `have to`: `Do` / `Does` + subject + `have to` + base verb
- question with `must` is rare and formal; use `have to` in speech
- past of `don't have to`: `didn't have to` + base verb
- no `do` or `does` is used with `must`

**When it applies**
- Prohibition: laws, signs, school and workplace rules, safety; signal words: `forbidden`, `not allowed`, `dangerous`
- No necessity: options, free things, things that other people already did; signal words: `free`, `optional`, `no need`

**When it does NOT apply** — `needn't` and `don't need to` also mean no obligation. `can't` can be used for a rule from another person, such as a sign. Test: does the speaker want to stop the action (use `mustn't`) or just say it is not required (use `don't have to`)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `don't have to` for a prohibition: the learner thinks both mean `not allowed`
- Using `mustn't` for a missing obligation
- Using `do` with `must`, or `to` after `must`
- Writing `doesn't has to` or `don't has to`: after `does` the verb is `have`

**Register and usage** — `Mustn't` is strong and direct, often on signs. In speech people often say `can't` or `not allowed to`.

rules.title: May and might for possibility
rules.description:
**The idea** — `may` and `might` say that something is possible but not sure. The speaker does not know. They are modal verbs, so they stay simple: one form, followed by a bare verb. `might` is a little less sure than `may`.

**The form**
- subject + `may` / `might` + base verb
- the same form for every person: no `-s`
- no `to` and no `-ing` after the modal
- negative: `may not` / `might not` + base verb
- question: asking about possibility is usually done with `Do you think ... might ...?`
- `maybe` (one word, adverb) goes at the start: no verb `be` needed after it
- `may be` (two words) = modal + verb `be`
- no `do` or `does` with these modals

**When it applies**
- Weather, plans and predictions you are not sure about
- Guesses about the present or the future; signal words: `perhaps`, `I'm not sure`, `I don't know`, `it's possible`
- Choices that are still open

**When it does NOT apply** — `will` and `be going to` express certainty or a firm plan. `can` expresses general ability or permission. Test: can the speaker say "maybe"? Use `may` or `might`. Does the speaker know it will happen? Use `will`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after the modal: the learner copies the pattern of normal verbs
- Adding `-s` after he, she, it
- Using `maybe` instead of `may be`, or using both together
- Using the past or `-ing` form after the modal
- Using `mayn't`: use `may not` or `might not`

**Register and usage** — `might` is common in everyday speech; `may` sounds a little more formal. The negative contraction `mightn't` is rare.

rules.title: Enough and too
rules.description:
**The idea** — `enough` and `too` describe the limit of an amount or a quality. `enough` means as much as needed; `too` means more than is good. Their position in the sentence is different, and learners often swap them or put them in the wrong place.

**The form**
- adjective or adverb + `enough`: `enough` comes after it
- `enough` + noun: `enough` comes before the noun
- `too` + adjective or adverb: `too` comes before it
- `too much` + uncountable noun; `too many` + countable plural noun
- `enough` / `too` + `to` + base verb: the result or purpose
- `too` + adjective + `for` + person + `to` + verb: someone else is the doer
- negative with `enough`: `not` + adjective + `enough` = too little
- never repeat the object pronoun after `to` + verb

**When it applies**
- Measuring a quality against a need: size, age, speed, temperature, price
- Counting amounts: time, money, chairs, food
- Explaining why something is impossible or possible; signal words: `can't`, `couldn't`, `so`

**When it does NOT apply** — `very` is a strong but neutral intensifier and does not suggest a result or a limit. `too` is negative; it always means a problem. Test: is there a problem or a limit? Use `too`. Is the amount sufficient? Use `enough`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Putting `enough` before an adjective: the learner copies the position of `too`
- Putting `enough` after a noun
- Using `too much` before an adjective: only `too` is needed
- Repeating the object after the infinitive
- Using `very` where `too` is needed

**Register and usage** — Neutral and very frequent in everyday talk.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `too` can also mean `also`, placed at the end

rules.title: Already, yet and still
rules.description:
**The idea** — These three adverbs show how an action relates to time and to our expectations. `already` says that something happened earlier than expected; `yet` asks or says that something expected has not happened up to now; `still` says that something continues. Each one has its own position and sentence type.

**The form**
- `already` + past participle, or between the auxiliary and the participle; also at the end for stress
- `already` is used in positive sentences and in surprised questions
- `yet` goes at the end of a negative sentence or a question
- `still` goes before the main verb, but after `be` and after the first auxiliary
- negative with `still`: `still` goes before `not` / `n't` for a surprise
- present perfect is typical with `already` and `yet`
- present simple or continuous is typical with `still`
- no `do` change: the adverbs do not affect the verb form

**When it applies**
- `already`: finished earlier than expected; signal: `so soon`, `by now`
- `yet`: waiting for something; signal: negatives and questions about results
- `still`: something goes on longer than expected; signal: `even now`, `after all this time`

**When it does NOT apply** — `yet` is not used in positive statements about the present; `still` is not used with a finished action. Test: is the action finished (`already` or `yet`) or does it continue (`still`)? In a positive sentence use `already`; in a negative or a question use `yet`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `already` in negatives instead of `yet`
- Using `yet` in a positive statement
- Putting `still` at the end of a sentence
- Using `still` with a finished action
- Putting `yet` before the verb

**Register and usage** — Neutral. In American English the past simple is also used with `already` and `yet`.

rules.title: Order of adjectives
rules.description:
**The idea** — When several adjectives describe one noun, English does not let them come in any order. Native speakers follow a fixed pattern, from the speaker's opinion to the material of the thing. The order sounds natural even though most people cannot say the rule aloud.

**The form**
- 1. opinion: beautiful, nice, expensive
- 2. size: big, small, tall
- 3. age: old, new, young
- 4. shape: round, square, flat
- 5. colour: red, blue, black
- 6. origin: Italian, Chinese, German
- 7. material: wooden, silk, leather
- the article or possessive comes before all adjectives

**When it applies**
- Descriptions of objects, people, places and food
- Two or more adjectives before a noun

**When it does NOT apply** — Adjectives from the same group can swap: they are joined by `and` or a comma. Test: say the list from left to right: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, then the noun.

**Typical mistakes**
- Putting colour before size: the learner follows the order of thinking
- Putting material or origin before age or colour
- Putting the opinion adjective next to the noun
- Making the adjective plural to agree with the noun

**Register and usage** — Natural in speech and writing. More than three adjectives sounds heavy and is avoided.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- A noun used as an adjective stays directly before the main noun

rules.title: Adjectives ending in -ed and -ing
rules.description:
**The idea** — Many adjectives come from verbs of feeling, and they exist in two forms. The `-ing` form describes the thing or the person that causes the feeling. The `-ed` form describes the person who has the feeling. Using the wrong one changes who is meant.

**The form**
- `-ing` adjective: the cause, the source of the feeling
- `-ed` adjective: the person (or animal) that feels
- both come after `be`, `feel`, `find`, `seem`, `look`, or before a noun
- no other ending: no plural, no agreement
- common pairs: bored and boring, interested and interesting, tired and tiring, excited and exciting, surprised and surprising, confused and confusing
- `-ed` adjectives are often followed by a preposition: `interested in`, `bored with`, `worried about`, `surprised at`
- after `-ing` adjectives there is usually no preposition
- negative and question forms are the normal ones for the verb `be`

**When it applies**
- Describing feelings: signal verbs such as `feel`, `be`, `get`
- Describing causes: films, books, lessons, news, jobs, trips, people

**When it does NOT apply** — An `-ed` form is also the past participle of a verb. In a verb phrase, such as the passive, it keeps its normal role. Test: is the word about a feeling inside a person? Use `-ed`. Is it about the thing that gives that feeling? Use `-ing`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `-ing` for the person who feels: the learner says what the person is, not what he feels
- Using `-ed` for the thing that causes the feeling
- Forgetting the usual preposition after `-ed` adjectives
- Adding an extra word (very, so) wrongly before a participle that works as a verb

**Register and usage** — Frequent in everyday talk. `very` is allowed with these adjectives; `much` is not.

rules.title: Stative verbs
rules.description:
**The idea** — Some verbs describe a state, not an action: what we think, feel, own or what something is. A state does not go on in steps, so these verbs do not normally appear in the continuous forms, even when the state is true now. The present simple is used instead.

**The form**
- stative verb + present simple: `know`, `knows`
- no `am` / `is` / `are` + `-ing` with these verbs
- negative: `do not` / `does not` + base verb
- question: `Do` / `Does` + subject + base verb
- verbs of thinking: know, understand, believe, remember, forget, think (opinion)
- verbs of feeling: like, love, hate, want, need, prefer
- verbs of possession and being: have (own), own, belong, contain, cost, mean
- verbs of the senses and appearance: seem, appear, sound, taste, smell, look (seem)

**When it applies**
- Present states, opinions and feelings
- The same rule in the past: use the simple form, not the past continuous
- Signal: the sentence describes a condition, not an event

**When it does NOT apply** — Some of these verbs have a second, active meaning and then can be continuous: `think` (consider), `have` (eat, take), `taste` (test), `see` (meet), `look` (watch). Test: can you replace the verb with `be` or `own`? Then it is a state and stays simple. If it describes an activity, the continuous is possible.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the continuous because the situation is happening now
- Using it for emotions such as `love` or `hate`
- Using it for `have` meaning own
- Copying a pattern from advertising slogans, where it is a special style

**Register and usage** — The continuous with `love` is used in informal speech for a new feeling, and in slogans. In learner English, avoid it.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `be` can be continuous when it describes behaviour: `being` + adjective

rules.title: No article in fixed expressions
rules.description:
**The idea** — Some everyday words are used without an article because they name an activity or a purpose, not a particular building or object. When we say that someone goes to school, we mean that they study; we do not mean the building. Many such fixed expressions also use a preposition.

**The form**
- `go to` / `be at` / `be in` + bare place noun: school, work, bed, church, prison, hospital, university
- `go home` / `be at home`: no `to` with `home`, no article
- `by` + vehicle: by bus, by car, by train, by plane, by bike, by taxi
- `on foot`: also without article
- meals: `have breakfast`, `have lunch`, `have dinner`
- times of day: `at night`, `at noon`, `at midnight`; but `in the morning`, `in the evening`
- seasons and days of the week often have no article in general statements: in summer, on Monday
- with a specific building or a modifier, the article returns: `the school` of our town

**When it applies**
- Daily routines: school, work, bed, meals, transport
- Purpose rather than place: study, work, sleep, pray, be treated, serve a sentence

**When it does NOT apply** — When you mean the building itself, or one particular place, use the article. Test: do you think about the activity (no article) or the physical object or place (`the`)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `the` to routine places: the learner treats them like ordinary nouns
- Adding `a` or `the` after `by` + vehicle
- Using `to` with `home`
- Using `in the night` instead of `at night`
- Adding an article to meals

**Register and usage** — Standard in all registers. British and American speakers differ with `hospital` and `university`, so learn the common fixed forms.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `in the evening` and `in the morning` keep `the`
- After a modifier the article returns: a good school, the same job

rules.title: Both, either and neither
rules.description:
**The idea** — These words talk about two things or two people. `both` means the two together; `either` means one of the two, it does not matter which; `neither` means none of the two. Each word has its own structure, and the verb agreement with them is a frequent problem.

**The form**
- `both` + plural noun, or `both of` + the / my / these + plural noun, with a plural verb
- `both ... and ...`: links two parts, with a plural verb for two subjects
- `either` + singular noun, or `either of` + plural, with a singular verb in formal use
- `either ... or ...`: offers a choice between two
- `neither` + singular noun, or `neither of` + plural, with a singular verb
- `neither ... nor ...`: negates both
- `neither` and `nor` already contain the negative: no extra `not`
- after a negative verb use `either`, not `neither`

**When it applies**
- Exactly two items: both hands, either side, neither parent
- Joining two nouns, adjectives or verbs with the paired word
- Short answers: `Neither.` `Either.` `Both.`

**When it does NOT apply** — For more than two, use `all`, `any` and `none`. Test: count the items. Two means this group of words; three or more means the other group.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using a singular verb with `both`
- Using a plural verb with `neither` or `either`
- Combining `neither` with a negative verb
- Using `both` with `or`, `either` with `and`, or `neither` with `or`
- Using `neither` and `nor` with a different grammatical form on each side

**Register and usage** — Neutral to formal. In speech the plural verb after `neither of` is common, but in writing the singular verb is preferred.

rules.title: As ... as for equality
rules.description:
**The idea** — To say that two things are equal in some quality, English puts the adjective or adverb between two `as`. This is the comparison of equality. The structure is fixed: the first `as` is an adverb of degree, the second `as` introduces the thing we compare with.

**The form**
- `as` + adjective + `as`: equal quality
- `as` + adverb + `as`: equal way of doing
- negative: `not as` + adjective + `as`, or `not so` + adjective + `as`
- the adjective stays in the basic form: no `-er`, no `more`
- after the second `as` a noun, a pronoun or a clause can follow
- pronoun after the second `as`: `as tall as I am` (formal) or `as tall as me` (informal)
- `as much` / `as many` + noun + `as`: equal amount
- `the same ... as` is a neighbour pattern with the noun: same size, same age

**When it applies**
- Comparing people, objects, places, amounts
- Signal words: `just as`, `twice as`, `not quite as`, `almost as`
- Emphasis on equality or on a difference in degree

**When it does NOT apply** — The comparative with `-er` / `more` + `than` shows inequality; `as ... as` shows equality. Test: are the things unequal (use `than`) or equal (use `as ... as`)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `than` instead of the second `as`: the learner copies the comparative
- Using `like` instead of the second `as`
- Putting a comparative form between the two `as`
- Using `that` instead of `as` for a clause
- Using `good` instead of `well` as an adverb of manner

**Register and usage** — Neutral. `Not so ... as` is a little more formal and old-fashioned.

rules.title: Be able to for ability
rules.description:
**The idea** — `can` has only two forms, present and a past form `could`. For all the other situations, such as the future, the present perfect or after another verb, English uses `be able to`. It is an ordinary phrase, built on the verb `be`, and means the same thing: having the ability or the chance to do something.

**The form**
- `be` + `able to` + base verb
- `be` takes the correct form for the subject and the tense: am, is, are, was, were, been, being
- future: `will be able to` + base verb
- present perfect: `have` / `has been able to` + base verb
- infinitive: `to be able to` + base verb, after verbs such as want, hope, need
- negative: `not able to` / `unable to`, with the right form of `be`
- question: the form of `be` + subject + `able to` + base verb
- `to` is part of the phrase, and the verb after it has no ending

**When it applies**
- Ability in tenses where `can` does not exist: future, perfect, infinitive, after a modal
- A single success in the past: `was able to` for one particular occasion
- Signal words: `after the course`, `by next year`, `so far`, `at last`

**When it does NOT apply** — In the present, `can` is shorter and more natural. For general past ability `could` is natural. Test: is `can` or `could` possible in this tense? If not, use `be able to`. For one specific success in the past, `was able to` is safer than `could`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `can` after another modal or `to`: `will can`, `to can`
- Using `can` in the present perfect
- Forgetting the form of `be`: `didn't able to`
- Leaving out `to`, or adding `-ing` or `-ed` after it

**Register and usage** — `be able to` sounds a little more formal than `can`. `unable to` is formal and typical of writing.

rules.title: The second conditional
rules.description:
**The idea** — The second conditional speaks about situations that are unreal, imaginary or very unlikely now. The speaker pictures a different world and says what would happen in it. The past form signals distance from reality, not past time.

**The form**
- `if` + past simple, `would` + base verb: `if I had`, `I would buy`
- With `be`, `were` is used for all persons in careful English: `if I were you`; `was` is common in speech
- Negative: `wouldn't` + base verb; `if` + `didn't` + base verb
- Question: `What would you do if you ...?`; `Would you ... if ...?`
- Other results: `could` or `might` instead of `would`
- Never use `would` in the `if` clause (`if I would have`)

**When it applies**
- Imaginary present or future situations: signal words `if I were`, `imagine`, `suppose`
- Giving advice: `if I were you`
- Unlikely future events: `if I won the lottery`

**When it does NOT apply** — For a real, possible future use the first conditional (`if` + present, `will`); for an imaginary past use the third conditional (`if` + past perfect). Test: if the situation is unreal or unlikely now or in the future, use the past after `if` and `would` in the result.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `would` in the `if` clause, because the result clause has it
- Using the present simple after `if`, which makes the situation real
- Using `will` in the result
- Using `is/was` instead of `were` in formal advice such as `if I were you`

**Register and usage** — `if I were you` is the fixed advice formula; both `was` and `were` occur in speech.

rules.title: The third conditional
rules.description:
**The idea** — The third conditional looks back at the past and imagines a different result. The speaker talks about something that did not happen and what would have followed. It is the form of regret, criticism and relief.

**The form**
- `if` + past perfect, `would have` + past participle: `had known`, `would have told`
- Contracted: `I'd have`, `hadn't`, `wouldn't have`
- Negative: `hadn't` + participle in the `if` part; `wouldn't have` + participle in the result
- Question: `What would you have done if ...?`
- Other results: `could have`, `might have` + participle
- Never use `would have` in the `if` clause (`if you would have asked`)

**When it applies**
- Unreal past situations: signal words `if only`, `I wish`, `too late`, `at that time`
- Regrets and criticism of past choices
- Explaining what a different event would have changed

**When it does NOT apply** — For an unreal present use the second conditional; for a possible future use the first. Test: if you look back at something that did not happen and can no longer change, use the past perfect after `if` and `would have` in the result.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `would have` in both clauses, because the result form is copied into the `if` clause
- Using the simple past after `if`, which sounds like the second conditional
- Using the base form or past form instead of the participle in the result (`would told`, `would have went`)
- Using `will have` in the result

**Register and usage** — In speech `'d` stands for both `had` and `would`; this is common and normal.

rules.title: Present perfect continuous
rules.description:
**The idea** — The present perfect continuous looks at an activity that started in the past and is still going on, or has just stopped with a visible result. It stresses the activity and its duration, not the finished result.

**The form**
- `have/has` + `been` + verb + `-ing`: `have been working`, `has been raining`
- Negative: `haven't/hasn't been` + `-ing`
- Question: `Have/Has` + subject + `been` + `-ing`; `How long have you been ...-ing?`
- Time with `for` (length) and `since` (start); `all day`, `lately`, `recently`
- Contracted: `I've been`, `she's been`
- State verbs (`know`, `like`, `have` for possession) do not take this form; use the simple perfect

**When it applies**
- An activity that began earlier and is still happening: signal words `for`, `since`, `how long`
- A recent activity with a present result: `I've been running`
- Repeated actions over a period: `lately`, `recently`, `all week`

**When it does NOT apply** — If you stress a completed result or a number (`have written three`), use the present perfect simple; for state verbs use the simple perfect too. Test: if the focus is on how long or on the activity, use the continuous; if it is on how much or on the result, use the simple.

**Typical mistakes**
- Dropping `been` or `-ing` (`have been wait`, `has raining`)
- Using the present continuous with `since` or `for` (`is working since 2019`), because the action is happening now
- Putting the subject in the wrong place in `how long` questions
- Using the continuous with state verbs (`have been knowing`)

**Register and usage** — It is frequent in speech to explain tiredness, delay or change.

rules.title: The past perfect
rules.description:
**The idea** — The past perfect marks an event that happened before another event in the past. It is the 'past in the past': the speaker is already telling about the past and needs to show which event came first.

**The form**
- `had` + past participle: `had finished`, `had gone`, `had seen`
- `had` is the same for all persons; contracted `I'd`, `she'd`
- Negative: `had not` (`hadn't`) + participle
- Question: `Had` + subject + participle: `had you eaten`
- Often with `already`, `just`, `never`, `before`, `by the time`, `after`, `until`
- Both events are usually in one sentence: past perfect for the earlier one, past simple for the later

**When it applies**
- Earlier of two past events: signal words `before`, `after`, `by the time`, `when`, `already`
- Reported speech about earlier events: `said he had seen`
- Explaining a past situation by an earlier cause
- Third conditional (`if I had known`)

**When it does NOT apply** — If the events follow each other in order and the order is clear, use the past simple for both. Test: if you need to show that one past event was completed before another, use the past perfect for the first; if you only list events in order, use the past simple.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the past simple for the earlier event, so the order is unclear
- Using the past perfect for both events
- Using `did` or `have` instead of `had` (`didn't have eaten`)
- Using the past form instead of the participle (`had went`)
- Placing `already` after the participle in the wrong position

**Register and usage** — It is typical of written narrative and of reports of earlier events.
rules.llmDescription: Past perfect had plus past participle for an event before another past event: past simple for the earlier event, had went, wrong event order, present perfect after reporting verb.

rules.title: The future perfect
rules.description:
**The idea** — The future perfect looks back from a point in the future and says that something will already be complete by then. The speaker stands in the future and sees an action behind them.

**The form**
- `will have` + past participle: `will have finished`, `will have gone`
- Contracted: `I'll have`, `she'll have`; negative: `won't have` + participle
- Question: `Will` + subject + `have` + participle: `will you have finished`
- Same form for all persons; no `-s`
- Time markers: `by` + time, `by the time`, `before`, `in two years`
- After `by the time` the verb is in the present simple, not `will`: `by the time you arrive`

**When it applies**
- A deadline for completion: signal words `by Friday`, `by then`, `by the end of the year`
- A prediction about completed events: `will have built`
- Guessing about something already done: `will have arrived`

**When it does NOT apply** — For an action that will simply happen at a future time, use `will` or `going to`; for an action in progress at that time, use the future continuous. Test: if the key idea is 'already finished by then', use the future perfect; if it is 'will happen then', use `will`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `have` (`will finished`), or using `has/had` instead
- Using the base form or the past form after `have` (`will have finish`)
- Using `will` after `by the time` (`by the time you will arrive`)
- Wrong question order: `will have you saved`
- Using the future simple where the completion by a deadline matters

**Register and usage** — It is common in planning, business and formal speech about deadlines.

rules.title: Modal verbs of deduction
rules.description:
**The idea** — English speakers show how sure they are about something with modal verbs. When they use evidence to guess, the choice of modal tells the listener how strong the conclusion is. The form also shows whether the guess is about now or about the past.

**The form**
- Present certainty: `must` + base verb (almost sure it is true)
- Present impossibility: `can't` + base verb (almost sure it is not true)
- Present possibility: `may`, `might`, `could` + base verb
- Past: modal + `have` + past participle: `must have left`, `can't have known`, `might have been`
- Continuous: modal + `be` + `-ing` (now) or `have been` + `-ing` (past)
- The opposite of `must` is `can't`, not `mustn't`; `mightn't` and `may not` mean it is possibly not true

**When it applies**
- Conclusions from evidence: signal words `probably`, `obviously`, `it seems`, `look at`
- Guessing about people, reasons and past events
- Hedging: `might`, `could`, `may` for weaker possibility

**When it does NOT apply** — For obligation or prohibition use `must/mustn't` in their rule sense; for ability use `can`. Test: if you are guessing from evidence, use `must/can't/might`; if you give a rule or a duty, use the obligation meaning.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after the modal or using `-s` (`must to be`, `might is`)
- Using the base form for past deductions (`must rained`) instead of `have` + participle
- Using `mustn't` or `can be not` for 'impossible'
- Using `can` for possible guesses where `might` is expected
- Writing `should of` or `must of` for `have`

**Register and usage** — `must have` and `might have` are common in everyday speech.

rules.title: Non-defining relative clauses
rules.description:
**The idea** — A non-defining relative clause adds extra information about a noun that is already clear. The noun does not need the clause to be understood, so the clause is separated from the rest of the sentence by commas, like a short aside.

**The form**
- Noun + comma + `who/which/whose/where/when` + clause + comma
- People: `who` or `whom`; things: `which`; possession: `whose`; places: `where`
- `that` is never used: only `who` and `which`
- The pronoun cannot be left out, even as an object
- `which` can refer to a whole idea before it: `he failed, which surprised us`
- With a preposition (formal): `in which`, `to whom`

**When it applies**
- Extra facts about names and unique things: signal words `Paris`, `my mother`, `the Nile`, `my laptop`
- Describing a noun that is already identified by a possessive, name or `this/that`
- Adding comments about a whole situation with `which`

**When it does NOT apply** — If the clause is needed to know which person or thing is meant, use a defining clause with no commas and possibly `that`. Test: if you can remove the clause and the noun is still clear, use commas and `who/which`; if not, no commas.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `that` after a comma, because `that` is common in defining clauses
- Leaving out the commas, which makes the clause look defining
- Repeating the noun with a pronoun (`which it is old`, `which I read it`)
- Using `who's` for `whose`
- Using `who` or `whom` after `which`-type nouns, mixing people and things

**Register and usage** — Mostly written and formal; in speech the commas are heard as pauses.

rules.title: Passive with modal verbs
rules.description:
**The idea** — When a modal verb (what is possible, necessary, allowed or advisable) is combined with a passive, English builds the passive after the modal. The modal stays first, and `be` carries the passive structure.

**The form**
- Present and future: modal + `be` + past participle: `must be finished`, `can be solved`, `will be served`
- Past: modal + `have been` + past participle: `could have been repaired`, `should have been told`
- Negative: `not` after the modal: `can't be done`, `shouldn't have been sent`
- Question: modal before the subject: `can the form be filled in`
- With `have to`, `ought to`, `need to`, `be going to`: `has to be done`, `ought to be sent`
- The modal never changes form; only the participle changes with the verb

**When it applies**
- Rules, duties and instructions: signal words `must be`, `has to be`, `should be`
- Possibility and ability: `can be seen`, `might be lost`
- Offers, promises and plans: `will be sent`, `is going to be built`
- Regret about past events: `should have been told`

**When it does NOT apply** — If the doer is the subject, use an active modal (`must finish it`). Test: if the thing receives the action and the doer is unknown or unimportant, put `be` + participle after the modal.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `be` (`must finished`), because the modal and participle seem enough
- Using the base verb or `-ing` instead of the participle (`can't be solve`, `has to be cleaning`)
- Writing `been` for the present or `be` for the past (`might been sold`)
- Putting `be` before the modal in questions

**Register and usage** — Common in instructions, reports and signs; it sounds impersonal and formal.

rules.title: Have something done
rules.description:
**The idea** — This structure says that someone arranges for another person to do a job for them, usually a service. It also describes bad things that happen to a person (a stolen bag, a broken window). The speaker is the receiver, not the doer, so the object comes before the past participle.

**The form**
- `have` + object + past participle — `have my hair cut`
- `have` changes for tense and person: `has`, `had`, `will have`, `is having`, `have had`
- Negative: `don't have` / `didn't have` + object + participle
- Question: `Do you have ...?`, `Did you have ...?` — the participle stays
- Informal: `get` + object + past participle, with the same order
- The participle never changes: `cut`, `repaired`, `done`
- `By` + doer can be added, but is rarely needed

**When it applies**
- Services: `cut`, `repair`, `paint`, `clean`, `service`, `deliver`, `test`
- Unwanted events: `stolen`, `broken`, `damaged`
- Signal words: `hairdresser`, `garage`, `dentist`, `workers`, `last week`

**When it does NOT apply** — If you do the job yourself, use the active verb. If you only describe what was done, use the passive. Test: ask "did I pay or arrange for someone?" — if yes, use `have something done`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the base form or `-ing` instead of the participle (`have my hair cutting`): learners think of a continuous action
- Putting the participle before the object, because the passive puts it first: `have done my hair`
- Using `do` with the main verb `have` incorrectly: `did you had`
- Using the active verb, which says you did the work yourself
- Using the wrong participle of an irregular verb

**Register and usage** — `Have` is neutral; `get` is informal and often used for unwanted events.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Have somebody do something` means "make or ask a person to do it"; no participle
- The same pattern with `want`, `need`: `I want it done`

rules.title: Reported questions
rules.description:
**The idea** — When you report a question, it stops being a question and becomes part of a statement. The helper verb and the inverted order of the direct question disappear, and the clause goes back to statement word order.

**The form**
- Reporting verb + question word or `if/whether` + subject + verb: `asked where I lived`
- Wh-questions keep the question word: `where`, `what`, `why`, `when`, `how much`
- Yes/no questions use `if` or `whether`: `asked if I was hungry`
- Statement order: subject before the verb; no `do/does/did`, no inversion
- Tenses shift back as in reported statements: present becomes past, `will` becomes `would`, `can` becomes `could`
- No question mark; pronouns and time words change to fit the new speaker

**When it applies**
- After `asked`, `wondered`, `wanted to know`, `enquired`
- In polite indirect questions: signal words `could you tell me`, `do you know`
- In reports of interviews, tests and conversations

**When it does NOT apply** — For the direct question use the question order with a helper verb; for a reported statement use `that`. Test: if the clause is inside another sentence, use statement order without `do/did`; if it stands alone, use question order.

**Typical mistakes**
- Keeping the question order (`asked where did I live`), because the idea is still a question
- Keeping `do/does/did` in the reported clause
- Using `that` instead of `if/whether` for yes/no questions
- Forgetting backshift
- Adding a question mark at the end

**Register and usage** — The same order is used for indirect polite questions in present time.
rules.llmDescription: Reported and indirect questions with statement word order: inverted order or do/did kept after asked, that instead of if or whether, missing backshift, question word order in a subordinate clause.

rules.title: Although, despite and however
rules.description:
**The idea** — Contrast words join two facts that seem not to go together. English has several of them, and each takes a different structure after it. Choosing the wrong structure makes a clause incorrect even if the meaning is clear.

**The form**
- `although` / `though` / `even though` + subject + verb, then a main clause (no `but`)
- `despite` / `in spite of` + noun or `-ing` form; there is no `of` after `despite`
- `despite the fact that` + subject + verb
- `however` + comma, at the start or inside a sentence, with a full stop or semicolon before it
- `but` joins two clauses with a comma: clause + `but` + clause
- `while` and `whereas` contrast two things in one sentence
- `even` strengthens only `though`, never `although`; `even` alone cannot join clauses

**When it applies**
- A surprising result: signal words `although`, `despite`, `in spite of`
- Two ideas set against each other: `however`, `but`, `whereas`
- A contrast in a long sentence or formal writing

**When it does NOT apply** — To give a reason use `because` or `so`; to add information use `and`. Test: if the second fact is surprising after the first, use a contrast word; if it follows naturally, use a reason or addition.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `but` together with `although`: one of them is enough, since both join the clauses
- Using `despite of` or `in spite` without `of`: only `in spite of` has `of`
- Using `despite` or `in spite of` with a full clause (`despite he was`): they need a noun or `-ing`
- Using `however` as a conjunction with a comma (`..., however ...`), which joins sentences wrongly
- Using `even` with `although` or `even` alone

**Register and usage** — `However` and `despite` are common in writing; `though` is more informal and can end a sentence.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Though` and `although` are often interchangeable; only `though` can go at the end
- `Whereas` compares two facts and does not mean surprise
rules.llmDescription: Contrast with although, though, even though, despite, in spite of, however, but: but after although, despite of, despite plus a clause, however joining clauses with a comma, even although.

examples.note: Despite is not followed by of.

rules.title: Separable phrasal verbs
rules.description:
**The idea** — A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word (a particle) that together have one meaning, often different from the verb alone. Many transitive phrasal verbs are separable: the object may stand between the verb and the particle. A pronoun object must stand there.

**The form**
- Separable: `verb` + object + `particle` — `turn the light off`
- Also allowed with a noun: `verb` + `particle` + object — `turn off the light`
- With a pronoun, only one order: `verb` + pronoun + `particle` — `turn it off`
- A long object goes after the particle
- Inseparable phrasal verbs keep the verb and particle together: `look after`, `take after`, `run into`, `get on with`
- Negative and question forms use the same positions: `throw it away`, `pick them up`
- Particles are `up`, `down`, `on`, `off`, `out`, `away`, `back`, `in`, `over`
- Passive form: the object becomes the subject

**When it applies**
- Action verbs with an object: `switch on`, `put on`, `pick up`, `give up`, `call off`
- A pronoun or short noun as the object
- Signal: the object is `it`, `them`, `him`, `her`, `me`, `us`

**When it does NOT apply** — Intransitive phrasal verbs have no object (`take off` of a plane, `get up`), and prepositional verbs keep the preposition before the object (`look after the baby`). Test: put the pronoun in; if the sentence still works only as `verb + it + particle`, it is separable.

**Typical mistakes**
- Putting the pronoun after the particle (`turn off it`): learners copy the noun pattern
- Splitting an inseparable verb (`looks her baby after`)
- Splitting an intransitive verb, which has no object
- Using the wrong particle, which changes the meaning completely

**Register and usage** — Phrasal verbs are very common in speech and informal writing; formal writing often prefers a single verb (`cancel` for `call off`).

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- Meaning can be literal (`pick up a pen`) or idiomatic (`pick up a language`)
- Some verbs have several meanings and different patterns

examples.correct: Don't throw them away, they are useful.

examples.correct: We put them on quickly before the rain.

examples.correct: She takes after her mother in many ways.

examples.correct: Please write it down before you forget.

rules.title: Remember, stop and try
rules.description:
**The idea** — A few verbs can be followed by either `to` + base verb or the `-ing` form, and the meaning changes with the pattern. `To` + verb looks forward to a purpose or a task; `-ing` looks back at an action or names the action itself. The wrong pattern says something different.

**The form**
- `remember to do` — not forget to do something that must be done
- `remember doing` — have a memory of something already done
- `forget to do` / `forget doing`: same contrast
- `stop to do` — stop in order to do something else
- `stop doing` — end an activity
- `try to do` — make an effort, perhaps without success
- `try doing` — test something to see what happens
- `regret to say` / `regret doing`: sorry to tell / sorry about the past

**When it applies**
- Reminders and duties: `remember to`, `don't forget to`
- Memories and regrets: `remember -ing`, `regret -ing`

**When it does NOT apply** — With verbs such as `like`, `start`, `begin` the two patterns mean almost the same. With `enjoy`, `finish`, `avoid` only `-ing` is possible; with `want`, `hope` only `to`. Test: ask whether the action is still to come (`to`) or already happened or in progress (`-ing`).

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the base form after `stop` (`stopped sing`)
- Using `-ing` for a future duty (`remember posting`): the duty has not happened yet
- Using `to` for a memory (`remember to meet her in 2010`)
- Using `stop to` for quitting a habit: that means stopping in order to do something
- Using `try to` for an experiment, such as a new recipe

**Register and usage** — Neutral. `Regret to inform` is formal.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Need` + `-ing` has a passive meaning (`needs repairing`)
- `Mean to do` is "intend"; `mean doing` is "involve"
rules.llmDescription: Verbs that change meaning with to or -ing: remember to/doing, forget to/doing, stop to/doing, try to/doing, regret to/doing, go on: wrong pattern for the intended meaning, base form after stop.

examples.note: News given now needs regret to.

examples.correct: The singer stopped singing and left the stage.

rules.title: Passive in continuous and perfect tenses
rules.description:
**The idea** — The passive puts the receiver of the action in the subject position. The same pattern works in every tense: only the form of `be` changes. In continuous and perfect tenses this means a chain of auxiliaries, and learners often lose one link of it.

**The form**
- present continuous passive: `am` / `is` / `are` + `being` + past participle
- past continuous passive: `was` / `were` + `being` + past participle
- present perfect passive: `have` / `has` + `been` + past participle
- past perfect passive: `had` + `been` + past participle
- future perfect passive: `will have been` + past participle
- the last verb is always the past participle (third form): built, sent, done
- agent with `by` is optional and added only when it is useful

**When it applies**
- Work in progress: repairs, building, cooking, cleaning (`being`)
- Results and news: signal words `already`, `yet`, `just`, `recently`, `since` (`been`)
- Earlier events in a past story (`had been`)
- When the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious

**When it does NOT apply** — With an active sentence the subject is the doer; the passive is only for the receiver. Test: is the subject doing the action (active) or receiving it (passive)? Then add the tense: for something in progress use `being`; for something completed use `been`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Forgetting `being` in the continuous passive
- Forgetting `been` in the perfect passive
- Using the base form or the past simple instead of the past participle
- Using `be` instead of `been`

**Register and usage** — Common in news, reports and instructions. Long chains such as `will have been` are rare in speech.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**

examples.correct: The bridge is being built now.

examples.correct: Our rooms were being painted when we came.
examples.note: Use the past participle after being.

rules.title: Unless and as long as
rules.description:
**The idea** — These conjunctions add a special meaning to a condition. `unless` means `if not`: the result happens in every case except one. `as long as`, `so long as`, `provided` and `providing` mean `only if`: the result happens only on one condition. They are used like `if` and follow its tense rule.

**The form**
- `unless` + subject + positive present simple verb, then the result clause
- `as long as` / `so long as` + subject + present simple
- `provided (that)` / `providing (that)` + subject + present simple
- the main clause is `will` + base verb, an imperative or a modal verb
- the conjunction clause can come first, with a comma, or second
- no negative after `unless`: the word already contains the negation
- no `will` in the conjunction clause for a future condition
- `on condition that` is a more formal neighbour with the same pattern

**When it applies**
- Exceptions: `unless` introduces the only case in which the result does not happen
- Limits and permissions: `as long as`, `provided` set a single requirement
- Contracts, rules, promises and warnings

**When it does NOT apply** — `if` is neutral and can introduce any condition; `unless` cannot be used when the condition is not the only exception, or for imagined situations with `would`. Test: can you replace the word with `if ... not`? Use `unless`. Can you replace it with `only if`? Use `as long as` or `provided`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding a negative after `unless`: the learner translates `if not` twice
- Using `will` in the conjunction clause
- Using `unless` where the meaning is `if` (a positive condition)
- Using `provided` for a negative condition
- Misplacing the auxiliary in an inverted way

**Register and usage** — `Unless` is neutral. `Provided` and `providing` are formal. `As long as` is neutral and common in speech.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Unless` is not used in questions with the same meaning as `if not`
rules.llmDescription: Conditionals with unless (if not), as long as, provided that (only if) + present tense; errors are negative after unless, will in the clause, unless meaning if.

examples.correct: Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus.

examples.correct: Unless we leave now, we will miss the train.

examples.note: Use normal word order after unless.

examples.correct: She will join us on condition she finishes work.
examples.note: Use the present after on condition.

rules.title: Purpose with so that and in order to
rules.description:
**The idea** — To say why someone does something, that is the aim of the action, English has several patterns. Each pattern requires a different structure after it: a bare infinitive after `to` and `in order to`, a full clause after `so that`. Using the wrong structure is a very common error.

**The form**
- `to` + base verb: the simplest purpose, when the subject is the same
- `in order to` + base verb: more formal, same subject
- `so as to` + base verb: formal, same subject
- negative: `in order not to` / `so as not to` + base verb; a bare `not to` is also possible
- `so that` + subject + `can` / `could` / `will` / `would` + base verb: a new subject or a clause
- `so that` + present simple is possible for a general present aim
- the modal follows the tense of the main verb: present aim with `can`, `will`; past aim with `could`, `would`
- never `for` + base verb, and never `for to`

**When it applies**
- Reasons for actions: why someone goes, writes, buys, learns
- Signal words: `why`, `in order`, `aim`, `goal`

**When it does NOT apply** — `for` + noun or `for` + `-ing` describes the use of a thing (a knife is for cutting), not the aim of a person. Test: is there a person who wants something (use `to` or `so that`) or is it the use of an object (use `for`)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `for` + base verb: the learner copies a native pattern
- Using `-ing` after `in order`
- Using `so that to`: two purpose markers together
- Missing the modal after `so that`
- Using the wrong tense of the modal

**Register and usage** — `To` is the most common in speech. `In order to` and `so as to` fit writing and formal speech.
rules.llmDescription: Purpose: to, in order to, so as to + bare infinitive, so that + clause with modal; errors are for to, in order + -ing, so that to.

rules.title: So ... that and such ... that
rules.description:
**The idea** — To show that a quality is so strong that it causes a result, English combines an intensifier with `that`. The intensifier is `so` or `such`, and the choice depends on what follows: `so` goes with an adjective or adverb, `such` goes with a noun phrase.

**The form**
- `so` + adjective or adverb + `that` + clause
- `so` + `many` / `much` / `few` / `little` + noun + `that` + clause
- `such` + `a` / `an` + adjective + singular countable noun + `that` + clause
- `such` + adjective + plural or uncountable noun + `that` + clause
- the result clause has its own subject and verb
- `that` can be dropped in speech
- negative result: `that` + negative clause
- never `so a`, and never `such` + bare adjective

**When it applies**
- Strong qualities with a result: so tired that, such a long day that
- Amounts: so much noise that, so many people that
- Descriptions of events, feelings, weather, people

**When it does NOT apply** — The result of purpose uses `so that` with a modal, and plain intensity without a result uses `so` or `such` alone. Test: what follows? If an adjective or adverb comes next, use `so`. If a noun, with or without adjectives, comes next, use `such`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `such` before an adjective only: the learner thinks `such` is the stronger `so`
- Using `so` before `a` + noun
- Using `than` or `what` instead of `that`
- Forgetting `many` or `much` after `so` with a noun
- Missing the verb in the result clause

**Register and usage** — Neutral. `that` is often omitted in speech. In writing it makes the result clear.
rules.llmDescription: Result clauses: so + adjective or adverb + that, such + (a) + adjective + noun + that; errors are so before a noun phrase, such before a bare adjective.

examples.correct: The coffee was so hot that I burned my tongue.

examples.correct: She has so many friends that her phone never stops.

examples.correct: There was such a loud noise that we jumped.

rules.title: The more ... the more
rules.description:
**The idea** — This pattern shows that two things change together: as one grows, the other grows or falls too. English puts a comparative in each half of the sentence and starts both halves with `the`. The two `the` words are not articles; they mark the link between the halves.

**The form**
- `The` + comparative + subject + verb, `the` + comparative + subject + verb
- comparative: adjective + `-er` (the harder), or `more` / `less` + adjective (the more careful)
- comparative of adverbs works the same way: the faster, the more slowly
- each half is a clause with its own subject and verb
- `be` can be dropped when the meaning is clear: the warmer the weather
- the first half is the cause or the condition; the second half is the result
- `the more` / `the less` alone can stand without an adjective
- word order in each half: normal subject + verb, no inversion

**When it applies**
- Parallel growth or decrease: age and wisdom, work and success, price and quality
- Signal words: `more and more` for a single growing quality; this rule for two connected qualities

**When it does NOT apply** — `more and more` describes one thing becoming stronger, and `than` compares two things. Test: are there two linked changes, one explaining the other? Use `the ... the ...`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out one or both `the`: the learner does not see that they are needed
- Using `most` for `more`
- Using a double comparative: `more higher`, `more cheaper`
- Inverting the verb and subject: `is the weather`
- Using `as ... as` for the same idea

**Register and usage** — Neutral in all registers; common in proverbs and in speech.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- Irregular comparatives stay irregular: the better, the worse, the further
rules.llmDescription: Linked comparatives the + comparative, the + comparative (the more ... the better); errors are missing the, most for more, double comparatives, inverted verb.

examples.wrong: More you practise, better you get.
examples.correct: The more you practise, the better you get.

examples.wrong: The more you practise, more confident you feel.
examples.correct: The more you practise, the more confident you feel.
examples.note: The second half needs the too.

examples.wrong: The most you read, the more you know.
examples.correct: The more you read, the more you know.

rules.title: The future continuous
rules.description:
**The idea** — The future continuous shows an action in progress at a particular moment in the future. The speaker imagines that moment as if it were already there and sees the action in the middle. It is also a polite way to ask about someone's plans without sounding like a request.

**The form**
- subject + `will` + `be` + verb + `-ing`
- `will` and `be` do not change for any person: no `-s`
- contraction: `I'll be`, `you'll be`, `he'll be`
- negative: `will not` / `won't` + `be` + verb + `-ing`
- question: `Will` + subject + `be` + verb + `-ing`
- short answers: `Yes, I will.` / `No, I won't.`
- `-ing` spelling: drop silent `e`, double a short final consonant
- `be going to be` + `-ing` is possible but rarer

**When it applies**
- A moment in the future: `at six tomorrow`, `this time next week`, `at midnight`, `in July`
- Actions that will be going on at a given moment
- Polite questions about plans: `Will you be using ...?`
- Plans that will happen in the normal course of events

**When it does NOT apply** — `will` + base verb expresses a decision, a promise or a prediction of a complete action. Test: picture one moment in the future. Is the action in the middle of happening then (future continuous) or is it a single, finished event (future simple)?

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `be`: the learner writes `will` + `-ing`
- Using `be` before `will` or the wrong form of `be`
- Using the base verb or `to` + verb after `be`
- Using `-ing` after `will` without `be`
- Using the form for a single finished action

**Register and usage** — Neutral. The polite question form is common in formal and business speech.
rules.llmDescription: Future continuous will be + -ing for an action in progress at a future moment (this time tomorrow); errors are will + -ing without be, will be + base verb.

examples.correct: The kids will be playing outside all day.

rules.title: The past perfect continuous
rules.description:
**The idea** — The past perfect continuous looks back from a moment in the past at an action that had been going on for some time before that moment. It stresses the length of the action or its visible result at the later moment, such as tiredness or wet ground.

**The form**
- subject + `had` + `been` + verb + `-ing`
- `had` is the same for every person: no `-s`
- contraction: `I'd been`, `she'd been`, `they'd been`
- negative: `had not` / `hadn't` + `been` + verb + `-ing`
- question: `Had` + subject + `been` + verb + `-ing`
- short answers: `Yes, I had.` / `No, I hadn't.`
- time expressions: `for` + length of time, `since` + starting point
- `-ing` spelling: drop silent `e`, double a short final consonant

**When it applies**
- A longer action before a past moment, with `for` or `since`
- An action that explains a result in the past: tiredness, a mess, wet streets
- A longer action before another past action; signal words: `when`, `before`, `by the time`, `until`

**When it does NOT apply** — The past perfect simple shows a finished action and focuses on completion; the past continuous shows an action in progress at the past moment itself. Test: was the action already going on before the past moment and lasting some time? Use the past perfect continuous. Was it only in progress at that moment? Use the past continuous.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the past simple instead of the perfect form
- Leaving out `been` or using `being`
- Using the base verb or the past form after `been`
- Using the present perfect continuous when the story is in the past
- Using `since` with a length of time

**Register and usage** — Neutral and common in storytelling and reports. Stative verbs do not take this form.
rules.llmDescription: Past perfect continuous had been + -ing for an action lasting up to a past moment (for, since, when I arrived); errors are past simple, missing been.

examples.correct: When I arrived, he had been waiting for an hour.
examples.note: The earlier long action needs had been + -ing.

examples.correct: She had been crying before I came.

examples.correct: We had been walking for hours.

examples.correct: He had been working there for five years.
examples.note: Use for with a length of time.

examples.correct: The ground was wet; it had been raining.

examples.correct: I hadn't been sleeping well before the trip.

examples.correct: She had been studying for hours, so she was exhausted.

examples.correct: They had been arguing when the police arrived.
examples.note: A past story needs had been, not have been.

rules.title: Inversion after negative adverbials
rules.description:
**The idea** — When a negative or restrictive adverbial opens the sentence for emphasis, English reverses subject and auxiliary verb, as in a question. The inversion gives the sentence a formal, dramatic tone.

**The form**
- Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb: `never have I seen`
- Adverbials: `never`, `rarely`, `seldom`, `hardly ... when`, `no sooner ... than`, `not only ... but also`, `little`, `under no circumstances`, `at no time`, `only after/when/if`
- If there is no auxiliary, add `do/does/did`: `rarely do we eat`, `little did they know`
- With `be`, invert directly: `not only was he late`
- The main verb after the auxiliary is the base form or participle, never inflected twice
- The second clause after `not only` and `hardly` keeps normal order
- `hardly/scarcely` + `had` ... `when`; `no sooner` + `had` ... `than`

**When it applies**
- Emphasis in formal writing and speeches: signal words `never`, `rarely`, `only then`, `under no circumstances`
- Strong surprise or warnings

**When it does NOT apply** — If the adverbial is not at the start, use normal order. Test: if the negative word opens the sentence for emphasis, invert the subject and the auxiliary; if it stays inside the clause, do not.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using normal order after the fronted adverbial (`never I have seen`), because the adverbial is treated like a simple opener
- Inverting without an auxiliary, or adding `do` where there is already another auxiliary
- Using the wrong tense pair in `no sooner` and `hardly`
- Inverting in the second half of `not only ... but`

**Register and usage** — Formal, literary or rhetorical; rare in casual speech.
rules.llmDescription: Inversion after fronted negative adverbials never, rarely, seldom, hardly, no sooner, not only, little, under no circumstances, only after: normal subject-verb order, missing do/did, inflected verb after the auxiliary.

examples.note: After 'not only' invert the subject and verb.

examples.correct: Seldom does he speak about his past.

examples.correct: At no time was the manager informed.
examples.note: After 'at no time' invert the verb.

rules.title: Mixed conditionals
rules.description:
**The idea** — Sometimes the condition and the result belong to different times. A mixed conditional links a past condition with a present result, or a present state with a past result. The tense of each clause follows its own time.

**The form**
- Past condition, present result: `if` + past perfect, `would` + base verb: `had studied`, `would be`
- Present or permanent condition, past result: `if` + past simple, `would have` + participle: `were taller`, `would have played`
- Negative: `hadn't` in the `if` part; `wouldn't` + base or `wouldn't have` + participle in the result
- Other modals in the result: `could`, `might`
- Time words show the mix: `now`, `today`, `still`, `by now` with the present result; `then`, `at that time` with the past result
- Never put `would` or `would have` in the `if` clause

**When it applies**
- A past event that still affects the present: signal words `now`, `today`, `still`, `by now`
- A permanent quality that would have changed the past: `if I were`, `if I weren't so`
- Regret and explanation

**When it does NOT apply** — If both parts are in the past, use the third conditional; if both are present or future, use the second. Test: ask 'when is the condition?' and 'when is the result?'; match each verb to its own time.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the same tense pattern in both clauses (`would have been a doctor now`), because the full third conditional is learned as one block
- Using `would` in the `if` clause
- Using `will` in the result
- Missing the participle after `would have`

**Register and usage** — Natural in discussion and reflection; neutral in tone.
rules.llmDescription: Mixed conditionals: past perfect condition with would plus base verb result now, or past simple condition with would have plus participle result: wrong tense pairing, would after if.

examples.correct: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
examples.note: A present result needs 'would' plus base verb.

examples.correct: If they weren't so lazy, they would have finished last week.

examples.correct: If she hadn't moved abroad, she would be here today.

examples.correct: If you were a better listener, you wouldn't have missed the details.

examples.correct: If I had saved more money, I could buy a house now.

rules.title: Wish and if only
rules.description:
**The idea** — `Wish` and `if only` express regret or a desire for something to be different from how it is. As in unreal conditionals, the verb moves one step back in time: the tense shows that the situation is not real, not that it is past.

**The form**
- Present situation: `wish` + past simple: `wish ... had`, `wishes ... were`
- Past situation: `wish` + past perfect: `wish ... had known`, `if only ... had listened`
- Annoyance or wanting change: `wish` + `would` + base verb: `wish ... would stop`
- Ability: `wish` + `could` + base verb; `if only` is stronger and more emotional
- `were` is used for all persons in careful English; `was` is common in speech
- `wish` itself is in the present; it does not change

**When it applies**
- Regret about now or the past: signal words `I wish`, `if only`, `too late`
- Complaints about other people's behaviour: `would`
- Desires that are impossible or unlikely

**When it does NOT apply** — For a real hope about the future use `hope` + present or `will`. Test: if the wish is about something unreal, use `wish` + past form; if it is a real possibility, use `hope`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the present form after `wish` (`wish ... have`), because the wish concerns the present
- Using `would` for oneself or for states (`wish ... would be`); `would` expresses annoyance about other people
- Using the past simple for a past regret
- Using `will` or `can` after `wish`
- Mixing up `wish` and `hope`

**Register and usage** — Natural in conversation and writing; `if only` is more emphatic.
rules.llmDescription: Wishes and regrets with wish and if only: present tense after wish, would for own states, past simple for past regret, will or can after wish.

examples.correct: I wish I had more free time.
examples.note: A present wish needs the past simple.

examples.correct: She wishes she were taller.

examples.correct: I wish you would stop shouting.

examples.correct: They wish they hadn't said that at the party.
examples.note: A past regret needs the past perfect.

rules.title: Would rather and it's time
rules.description:
**The idea** — Some expressions of preference and urgency use a past form to talk about the present or future. The past form does not mean past time; it shows that the situation is unreal or not yet true. The same idea lies behind `wish` and the second conditional.

**The form**
- Preference of the speaker: `would rather` + base verb — `rather stay`
- Preference about another person: `would rather` + subject + past simple — `rather you stayed`
- Regret about the past: `would rather` + subject + past perfect
- Comparison: `would rather` + base verb + `than` + base verb (no `to`)
- Negative: `would rather not` + base verb; `would rather` + subject + `didn't` + base verb
- It is time: `it's time` + subject + past simple — `time we left`
- Stronger: `it's high time`, `it's about time` + subject + past simple
- The past form refers to now or the future; `were` can replace `was` after `I`, `he`, `she`

**When it applies**
- Saying what you prefer other people to do
- Saying that something should already have started or happened

**When it does NOT apply** — If the subject of both verbs is the same, use `would rather` + bare verb with no past form. Test: same person → bare verb; different person → past simple.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the present after `would rather` + another subject, because learners expect a present meaning
- Adding `to` after `would rather`
- Using the present after `it's time` + subject
- Using `will` or `would` in the second clause
- Using `to` before the second verb after `than`

**Register and usage** — Natural in speech and writing. `It's high time` expresses criticism or impatience.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- `Would sooner` has the same pattern as `would rather`
- `It's time` + `-ing` is not used

examples.correct: Would you rather I closed the window?
examples.note: Use the past simple after rather I.

rules.title: The mandative subjunctive
rules.description:
**The idea** — After verbs and adjectives that express a demand, suggestion, recommendation or necessity, formal English uses the bare base form of the verb in the that-clause. The clause names something that should happen, not something that happens, so the verb does not carry person, number or tense.

**The form**
- `that` + subject + base verb: `suggested that he take`, `insist that she be`
- The same form for all persons: no `-s`, no `-ed`, no `will`
- Negative: `not` before the verb, with no `do`: `that he not accept`
- Passive: `be` + participle: `that the fee be paid`
- Triggers: `suggest`, `recommend`, `demand`, `insist`, `require`, `propose`, `request`, `ask`
- Adjectives and nouns: `essential`, `vital`, `important`, `necessary`, `it is vital that`, `the requirement that`
- `that` can be omitted after verbs

**When it applies**
- Formal advice, rules and decisions: signal words `recommend that`, `insist that`, `essential that`
- Meetings, contracts, regulations and academic writing

**When it does NOT apply** — British informal English often uses `should` + base verb or the ordinary indicative instead. Test: if the that-clause states a required or recommended action, the bare verb form is available; if it reports a fact, use a normal tense.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `-s` after `he/she` (`that he takes`), because normal agreement is applied
- Using `is/was` instead of `be` (`that she is present`)
- Using `don't/doesn't` for the negative instead of bare `not`
- Using `will` or `would` inside the clause

**Register and usage** — Formal and written; `should` + base verb is the British alternative, and both are correct.
rules.llmDescription: Mandative subjunctive: bare base verb in that-clauses after suggest, recommend, insist, demand, require, essential, vital; -s, is/was or do-negation used instead of the bare form.

rules.title: Cleft sentences with it
rules.description:
**The idea** — A cleft sentence splits one idea into two clauses so that one part gets strong emphasis. The `it is ... that` frame places the focus word or phrase between `it is/was` and a relative-like clause, to correct, contrast or highlight.

**The form**
- `it` + `is/was` + focus + `that/who` + clause: `it was Anna who`
- Focus can be a subject, an object, an adverbial of time, place or reason, or a phrase
- Use `who` or `that` for people, `that` for things and for adverbials; `what` is never used
- The verb after `who/that` agrees with the focus when the focus is the subject
- `be` agrees with tense, not with the focus; the singular `it was` stays even before plural nouns
- Negative focus: `it wasn't the price that`
- Question: `Was it you who ...?`

**When it applies**
- Correcting a wrong idea: signal words `it was ... not ...`, `it is because of`
- Stressing time, place or cause: `it was in Paris that`, `it was not until midnight that`
- Highlighting a person or object in writing

**When it does NOT apply** — To emphasise a whole action or a thing as a description, use the pseudo-cleft with `what` (`what I need is`). Test: if you highlight one named element from a clause, use `it is ... that`; if you highlight the whole clause with `what`, use the pseudo-cleft.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `what`, `which` or `when` instead of `that` or `who` (`it was Anna what`)
- Using the wrong word order after `that` (`that were we married`); the clause keeps statement order
- Making `be` plural with a plural focus
- Dropping `that` after `not until`

**Register and usage** — Common in formal writing and careful speech.
rules.llmDescription: Cleft sentences it is or it was plus focus plus who or that: what, which or when instead of that, wrong word order after that, missing that after not until.
